options.label: The degree to which individuals tend to associate in social groups
options.feedback: Correct. Sociality measures how much animals group together and cooperate.

options.label: The ability to solve problems using innovation
options.feedback: That is a characteristic some social animals have, but it is not the definition of sociality.

options.label: The care a parent gives to its own offspring
options.feedback: That is parental investment, which is one trait within sociality, not sociality itself.

options.label: The desire to mate and reproduce
options.feedback: Mating is a basic interaction, not what defines sociality, which involves associating beyond that.

items.ok_line: Sociality is about how much animals group and cooperate.
items.exp_text: Sociality is the degree to which individuals in an animal population tend to associate in social groups and form cooperative societies. It is a broad measure, from solitary living to full eusociality.

options.label: The time an animal spends finding a mate
options.feedback: Finding a mate is part of reproduction, but parental investment specifically concerns caring for offspring.

options.label: The energy an animal uses to defend its territory
options.feedback: Territory defense is not parental investment; that term is about spending resources on one's own young.

options.label: Any expenditure of resources to benefit one's offspring
options.feedback: Correct. Parental investment is spending time, energy, or social capital to help one's offspring survive.

options.label: The act of building a nest for future young
options.feedback: Building a nest might be part of it, but parental investment is the general spending of resources on offspring.

items.ok_line: Parental investment is spending resources on your young.
items.ko_line: Think about what parents do for their own offspring.
items.exp_text: Parental investment is any expenditure of resources—time, energy, or social capital—to benefit one's offspring. It is the most fundamental characteristic of animal sociality, and it detracts from a parent's ability to invest in future reproduction or aid to kin.

items.prompt: What is the highest degree of sociality recognized?

options.label: Presociality
options.feedback: Presociality is below eusociality; it includes animals with some social traits but not all.

options.label: Eusociality
options.feedback: Correct. Eusociality is the highest degree, with overlapping generations, reproductive division of labor, and cooperative care of young.

options.label: Subsociality
options.feedback: Subsociality is a lower level, involving only parental care without other social traits.

options.label: Parasociality
options.feedback: Parasociality is a middle group between subsocial and eusocial, so it is not the highest.

items.ok_line: Eusociality is the top level of sociality.
items.ko_line: There is a higher social degree than that.
items.exp_text: Eusociality is the highest degree of sociality. A eusocial group shows overlapping adult generations, reproductive division of labor, and cooperative care of young, and in the most refined cases, a biological caste system.

items.prompt: What does a subsocial animal do?

options.label: It lives completely alone, only meeting to mate
options.feedback: That is a solitary animal, not subsocial. Subsocial animals care for their young.

options.label: It lives in a large colony with many generations together
options.feedback: That is eusociality, which has more than just parental care.

options.label: It nests with other adults but each cares for its own young
options.feedback: That is communal living, not subsociality.

options.label: It cares for its young for some length of time
options.feedback: Correct. A subsocial animal cares for its own offspring but shows no other social traits.

items.ok_line: Subsocial animals care for their young.
items.ko_line: Subsociality is specifically about parental care.
items.exp_text: A subsocial animal cares for its young for some period of time, even if short, but does not associate with other adults beyond that. It is the simplest form of sociality, beyond just mating.

items.prompt: What is the main difference between communal and quasisocial animals?

options.label: Communal animals each care for their own young, while quasisocial animals share brood care
options.feedback: Correct. In communal groups, adults cohabit but care for their own young; in quasisocial groups, they share care of the brood.

options.label: Communal animals have a caste system, while quasisocial animals do not
options.feedback: A caste system is found in semisocial and eusocial animals, not in communal or quasisocial.

options.label: Communal animals live alone, while quasisocial animals live together
options.feedback: Both communal and quasisocial animals cohabit in a single nest; the difference is in who cares for the young.

options.label: Communal animals are solitary, while quasisocial animals are social
options.feedback: Both are parasocial, meaning they live in cooperative dwellings; the difference is about young care.

items.ok_line: Communal keeps young care separate; quasisocial shares it.
items.ko_line: Look at how each group handles the young.
items.exp_text: In a communal group, adults cohabit in a single nest but each cares for its own young. In a quasisocial group, adults cohabit and also share the responsibilities of brood care. This is the defining difference between the two.

options.label: A population where adults only mate and then separate
options.feedback: That is solitary behavior, not semisocial.

options.label: A population where parents care for their own young in a shared nest
options.feedback: That is communal, not semisocial.

options.label: A population with communal living, shared brood care, and a caste system
options.feedback: Correct. Semisocial groups have the features of communal and quasisocial, plus a biological caste system.

options.label: A population with overlapping generations and cooperative care
options.feedback: That is eusocial, which goes beyond semisocial.

items.ok_line: Semisocial adds a caste system on top of sharing.
items.ko_line: Think about what extra trait semisocial has.
items.exp_text: A semisocial population has the features of communal and quasisocial populations—cohabiting and sharing brood care—but also has a biological caste system that delegates labor based on whether an individual can reproduce. It sits between quasisocial and eusocial.

items.prompt: Which animals are common examples of eusociality?

options.label: Jaguars and tigers
options.feedback: These are solitary cats, not eusocial.

options.label: Ants, bees, and termites
options.feedback: Correct. Hymenoptera like ants and bees, and termites (Blattodea), are classic eusocial insects.

options.label: Lions and spotted hyenas
options.feedback: These are social predators, but they are not eusocial; they lack caste systems and overlapping generations in the same way.

options.label: Orangutans and mouse lemurs
options.feedback: These are solitary-but-social primates, not eusocial.

items.ok_line: Ants, bees, and termites are eusocial.
items.ko_line: Those animals are social differently, but not eusocial.
items.exp_text: Common eusocial animals come from Hymenoptera—ants, bees, sawflies, and wasps—and from the infraorder Isoptera, which includes termites. They show the full set of eusocial traits.

items.prompt: What is a key feature of a eusocial society?

options.label: Overlapping adult generations
options.feedback: Correct. Eusocial groups have more than one adult generation alive at the same time, and older generations help care for the youngest.

options.label: Adults live alone except for mating
options.feedback: That is solitary living, the opposite of eusocial.

options.label: Only one adult generation is alive at a time
options.feedback: Eusociality requires overlapping generations, not just one.

options.label: Each adult cares only for its own offspring
options.feedback: In eusocial groups, care is cooperative, shared among members, not individual.

items.exp_text: Eusocial societies have three main traits: overlapping adult generations, cooperative care of young, and division of reproductive labor. Overlapping generations means more than one adult generation lives together and older ones help care for the newest offspring.

options.label: An animal that always lives in large groups
options.feedback: That is social, not solitary-but-social.

options.label: An animal that never meets others of its kind
options.feedback: Solitary-but-social animals do interact, just not in groups for foraging.

options.label: An animal that only comes together to mate
options.feedback: That is a solitary animal; solitary-but-social animals share sleeping spots or nests.

options.label: An animal that forages alone but sleeps with others
options.feedback: Correct. They feed separately but some individuals share sleeping locations or nests.

items.ko_line: Check how they behave when not feeding.
items.exp_text: Solitary-but-social animals forage separately, but some individuals sleep in the same location or share nests. They are between solitary and fully social, common among some primates and other mammals.

items.prompt: What do eusocial snapping shrimp, like Synalpheus regalis, have in common with ants?

options.label: They all live solitary lives
options.feedback: No, they live in colonies with many members.

options.label: They all hunt in coordinated packs
options.feedback: They don't hunt together; they live in a shared space and defend it.

options.label: They live in a group with one breeding female and many defenders
options.feedback: Correct. Like eusocial insects, they have a single breeding female and non-breeding members defend the colony.

options.label: They all build large above-ground mounds
options.feedback: Shrimp live in sponges and reefs, not mounds.

items.ok_line: One breeder, many defenders, shared home.
items.ko_line: Think about their social structure, not hunting.
items.exp_text: Synalpheus regalis are eusocial snapping shrimp that live in groups in a restricted area, often inside sponges. Each group has one breeding female, protected by many male defenders with enlarged claws, and they share a single living space—similar to eusocial insect colonies.
